evidence.title: Implementation of a clinical decision support tool for hypertension in a rural health system
evidence.venue: Journal of the American Medical Informatics Association : JAMIA
evidence.outcome: Repeat BP measurement and hypertension recognition by implementation intensity
evidence.effect: In-person and online training plus monthly check-ins and feedback versus online-only training: repeat BP measurement aOR 3.45; 1.88-6.33; hypertension recognition aOR 2.31; 1.08-4.98. Training effects were not isolated from implementation support.
evidence.quote: High-intensity implementation was more effective than low-intensity implementation for repeat BP measurement (aOR 3.45; 1.88-6.33) and hypertension recognition (aOR 2.31; 1.08-4.98).

evidence.title: Assessment of the Efficiency of a ChatGPT-Based Tool, MyGenAssist, in an Industry Pharmacovigilance Department for Case Documentation: Cross-Over Study
evidence.outcome: Training burden and time savings after brief tool-specific training for pharmacovigilance team
evidence.effect: A 2-hour training session sufficed for implementation; 23.3% (95% CI 13.8%-32.8%) time saving per case (P<.001).
evidence.quote: The implementation of MyGenAssist for this activity only required a 2-hour training session for the pharmacovigilance team.

evidence.title: Deploying Artificial Intelligence for Thoracic Imaging Around the World
evidence.venue: Journal of the American College of Radiology : JACR
evidence.outcome: Change in knowledge test scores after introduction-to-AI course
evidence.effect: 30 participants; average pre-knowledge test score 75%, posttest score 95%.
evidence.quote: Thirty participants completed the introduction-to-AI course with an average pre-knowledge test score of 75% and an average posttest score of 95%.

evidence.title: Computer-Aided Detection for Chest Radiography to Improve the Quality of Tuberculosis Diagnosis in Vietnam's District Health Facilities: An Implementation Study
evidence.outcome: Physician-CAD CXR concordance and Xpert referral/yield over time alongside physician training
evidence.effect: Concordance of physician and CAD TB-presumptive CXRs rose from 47.3% at three months to 76.1% at nine months; Xpert-confirmed TB per 100,000 CXRs rose from 858 to 2112. No comparison group.
evidence.quote: Concordance between physician and CAD CXR results improved with training and was important to optimize Xpert testing.

evidence.title: Primary care clinician engagement in implementing a machine-learning algorithm for targeted screening of familial hypercholesterolemia
evidence.outcome: Clinician FH knowledge following bundled education and clinical decision-support implementation
evidence.effect: Following the bundled intervention, respondents correctly answering at least 2/3rds of FH knowledge questions increased from 40 to 65 %. Surveys included n = 55 at baseline and n = 23 at follow-up; comparisons were unpaired.
evidence.quote: Objective PCC knowledge scores improved from 40 to 65 % of responders correctly responding to at least 2/3rds of survey questions.

evidence.title: Targeted Interventions Lead to Quality Improvement in Year 2 of an Artificial Intelligence-Based Diabetic Retinopathy Detection Program in Northern California
evidence.outcome: AI image gradability and patient encounters after training-based intervention framework
evidence.effect: Gradability rose from 62.3% in Year 1 to 71.2% in Year 2; patient encounters increased by 21.9%. Uncontrolled pre-post comparison.
evidence.quote: Interventions, including enhanced training protocols and camera utilization reports, effectively improved screening efficiency.

evidence.title: Academic Detailing to Enhance Adoption of Clinical Decision Support for Patients at Risk of Opioid Overdose
evidence.outcome: Naloxone prescription-to-alert ratio after educational email to all providers
evidence.effect: Ratio rose from 32.6% to 51.7%, a 19.1% absolute increase (95% CI 16.3-21.9%, p<0.001) over about 8 months before vs after.
evidence.quote: The first academic detailing intervention resulted in a prescription-to-alert ratio increase from 32.6 to 51.7%, a 19.1% absolute increase when comparing the approximately 8 months before and after the email was sent (95% confidence interval [CI]: 16.3-21.9%, p < 0.001).

evidence.title: Enhancing Physicians' Adherence to the 2023 Sudan Malaria Case Management Protocol Using AI as an Intervention Tool
evidence.outcome: Physician knowledge and questionnaire-assessed adherence to malaria case-management guidelines
evidence.effect: AI-CDSS plus targeted training increased mean compliance from 50.7% (95% CI: 42-59) to 96.8% (95% CI: 92-100, p<0.001); the independent effect of training was not isolated.
evidence.quote: Mean compliance increased from 50.7% (95% CI: 42-59) to 96.8% (95% CI: 92-100, p<0.001).

evidence.title: Evaluating the usability and practicality of AI-enabled smartphone-based obstetric ultrasound in Sierra Leone: a mixed-methods study
evidence.outcome: Sufficient scan quality with vs without in-app tutorial videos
evidence.effect: Tutorial-equipped app associated with higher scan quality (OR 14.1, 95% CI 6.40–31.12); first-time users 84.6% vs 31.0% sufficient (OR 12.2, 95% CI 4.11–36.32); confounded with facility type
evidence.quote: Bivariate results showed a strong positive association between the use of an app with tutorial videos and scan quality (OR: 14.1, 95% CI: 6.40–31.12, p < 0.001).

evidence.title: Boosting LLM-Assisted Diagnosis: 10-Minute LLM Tutorial Elevates Radiology Residents’ Performance in Brain MRI Interpretation
evidence.outcome: Resident diagnostic accuracy and confidence with vs without a 10-minute LLM tutorial
evidence.effect: Top-three accuracy 62.5% (55/88) after tutorial vs 44.8% (39/87) LLM without tutorial and 32.2% (28/87) conventional search; tutorial gave higher scores (binary p=0.042, numeric p=0.016) and confidence (p=0.006).
evidence.quote: The LLM tutorial led to significantly higher performance (binary scores: p = 0.042, numeric scores: p = 0.016) and confidence (p = 0.006) but resulted in no relevant differences in reading times.

evidence.title: Potential of E-Learning Interventions and Artificial Intelligence-Assisted Contouring Skills in Radiotherapy: The ELAISA Study
evidence.outcome: Effect of a teaching session on contouring quality and time savings with AI
evidence.effect: Teaching increased DSC for only two OARs without AI, but increased AI time savings (e.g., mandible -9.41 min with teaching vs -6.60 without); effect persisted at 6 months.
evidence.quote: Although teaching did not increase contouring quality as much as expected, teaching modified the time savings of AI-assisted contouring; for most OARs, AI-assisted contouring alone reduced contouring time (crosses, Fig 5 ), but even larger time savings were observed when AI-assisted contouring was combined with teaching (lines, Fig 5 ).
evidence.country: Multiple low- and middle-income countries (23 institutions, IAEA); cases from Denmark

evidence.title: Effectiveness of Informed AI Use on Clinical Competence of General Practitioners and Internists: Pre-Post Intervention Study
evidence.outcome: clinical decision-making test performance
evidence.effect: Scores improved 56.88% (SD 15.65%) to 77.56% (SD 12.71%), mean difference 20.68%; pass rate 6.4% to 58.6%; P<.001.
evidence.quote: The mean score improved from 56.88% (SD 15.65%) to 77.56% (SD 12.71%), with a mean difference of 20.68% ( P <.001).
evidence.country: Multinational (39 countries; highest participation from Saudi Arabia, Syria, Egypt, Algeria, Jordan)

evidence.title: Educational Impact of a National Training Webinar on AI-based Automatic Contouring in Radiation Oncology
evidence.venue: Journal of cancer education : the official journal of the American Association for Cancer Education
evidence.outcome: Pre- vs post-webinar knowledge score on AI auto-contouring (5-item MCQ)
evidence.effect: Median score rose from 3.5 (IQR 2–4) to 5.0 (IQR 4–5), p < 0.0001, among 28 participants.
evidence.quote: The median questionnaire score increased from 3.5 (IQR: 2–4) before training to 5.0 (IQR: 4–5) after training, corresponding to a statistically significant improvement (p < 0.0001).

evidence.title: Patient and dental practitioner acceptance of artificial intelligence in dental care: a cross-sectional study in Saudi Arabia's eastern province
evidence.outcome: Association of formal AI training with practitioners' perceived accuracy, patient satisfaction, and clinical outcomes
evidence.effect: Formal AI training was significantly associated with higher perceived decision-making accuracy (p = 0.019), patient satisfaction (p = 0.017), and clinical outcomes (p = 0.012). These are self-reported perceptions, not measured safe-use outcomes.
evidence.quote: Formal AI training was associated with higher perceived scores among dental practitioners highlighting the potential value of educational initiatives in fostering AI adoption.

evidence.title: Evaluating Training Effectiveness for a Technology-Driven Pain Assessment Application: A Cross-Sectional Study
evidence.venue: Pain management nursing : official journal of the American Society of Pain Management Nurses
evidence.outcome: Satisfaction, confidence, and knowledge after one-hour pre-use tool-specific training
evidence.effect: 94.7% satisfied and confident to use the app; 52.6% wanted more post-training support; correct knowledge scores varied 36.8% to 84.2%.
evidence.quote: Most respondents were satisfied with the training and confident to use the application (94.7%).

evidence.title: GenAI in Occupational Therapy: A Survey of Adoption, Ethical Concerns, and Training Needs
evidence.outcome: Proportion of practitioners who received GenAI training and desire for training
evidence.effect: 42.2% reported receiving no training; 68.3% believed practitioners should receive GenAI training; 73.2% desired formal webinar-based instruction.
evidence.quote: While 68.3% believed practitioners should receive GenAI training, 42.2% reported receiving no training, with most (73.2%) desiring formal webinar-based instruction.

evidence.title: Don’t set and forget: Optimising Digital Early Warning Tools through upgrade and evaluation
evidence.outcome: User awareness of tool functionality and training needs
evidence.effect: Focus groups and surveys identified lack of awareness of specific functionality and a need for training; no numerical estimates were reported.
evidence.quote: Stakeholder focus groups and surveys identified a lack of awareness of specific functionality, issues with alert fatigue, technical challenges with the system, the need for training and concerns around over-reliance on the system by junior staff.

evidence.title: Perceptions and Adoption of Generative Artificial Intelligence Among Physical Therapy Professionals in Ohio: A Cross-Sectional Survey
evidence.outcome: Receipt of AI training (prompt development) among respondents
evidence.effect: No training in AI prompt development: 81.8% of PTs and 84.5% of PTAs.
evidence.quote: More than half of respondents reported no formal workplace AI policy (PTs: 54.4%; PTAs: 60.6%), and the vast majority had received no training in AI prompt development (PTs: 81.8%; PTAs: 84.5%).

evidence.title: Knowledge, Attitudes, and Use of Artificial Intelligence Among Adult and Pediatric Hematologists in Türkiye: A National Cross- Sectional Survey
evidence.outcome: Receipt of structured AI training among clinical AI users
evidence.effect: 87% reported clinical AI use in prior three months, yet only 14% had received structured AI training.
evidence.quote: Clinical AI use in the prior three months was reported by 87%, yet only 14% had received structured AI training.

evidence.title: Artificial Intelligence Adoption in Dental Healthcare Institutions in the United Arab Emirates: A Cross-Sectional Study of Professional Perceptions, Organizational Readiness, and Healthcare Quality
evidence.outcome: Perceived adequacy of prior AI training and institutional training resources among dental professionals
evidence.effect: Adequate previous AI training mean 3.06 and institutional training resources mean 3.10, versus support for further AI training mean 4.13; AI awareness and training was the lowest construct (3.45).
evidence.quote: Participants strongly supported further AI training (mean = 4.13), despite lower ratings for adequate previous AI training (mean = 3.06) and institutional training resources (mean = 3.10).

evidence.title: Perspectives of Medical Imaging Professionals about the Impact of AI on Swiss Radiographers
evidence.outcome: Perceived preparedness and availability of AI-specific training among imaging professionals
evidence.effect: 68.3% did not feel well trained/prepared to implement AI in practice; 87.6% noted non-availability of specific training; 93% said AI education should be in undergraduate programs.
evidence.quote: Participants (68.3%) did not feel well trained/prepared to implement AI in their practice, highlighting the non-availability of specific training (87.6%).

evidence.title: Knowledge and perception of primary care healthcare professionals on the use of artificial intelligence as a healthcare tool
evidence.outcome: Proportion of primary care professionals who had received AI training and wanted training
evidence.effect: 65.8% had not received any AI training; 91.4% would like to receive training.
evidence.quote: 65.8% indicated that they had not received any AI training and 91.4% that they would like to receive training.
evidence.sample_unit: primary care physicians and nurses (survey respondents)

evidence.title: Implementing a Machine Learning Screening Tool for Malnutrition: Insights From Qualitative Research Applicable to Other Machine Learning-Based Clinical Decision Support Systems
evidence.outcome: Registered dietitians' depth of understanding of the ML tool across hospitals and levels
evidence.effect: Depth of tool understanding varied by hospital and level among 17 interviewed registered dietitians; continuous stakeholder involvement at new sites was judged vital given staff turnover.
evidence.quote: (5) depth of tool understanding varied by hospital and level;

evidence.title: Experiences Regarding Use and Implementation of Artificial Intelligence-Supported Follow-Up of Atypical Moles at a Dermatological Outpatient Clinic: Qualitative Study
evidence.outcome: Barriers to consistent use of AI total body dermoscopy module, including training gaps
evidence.effect: Lack of guidance, time pressure, and insufficient training were barriers to consistent use; only 3 of 14 participants had actual experience using the TBD module.
evidence.quote: First, several organizational matters were revealed to be a barrier to consistent use of the ATBM Master's TBD module, namely lack of guidance, time pressure, and insufficient training.

evidence.title: Nordic radiographers' and students' perspectives on artificial intelligence - A cross-sectional online survey
evidence.outcome: Proportion of radiographers who received AI training in clinical practice
evidence.effect: 43% (n = 254) had not received any AI training in clinical practice; 13% (n = 76) received AI content in undergraduate training; 77.9% (n = 412) interested in AI education.
evidence.quote: A total of 43% (n = 254) of the respondents had not received any AI training in clinical practice.
evidence.country: Nordic countries (Denmark, Norway, Sweden, Iceland, Greenland, Faroe Islands)

evidence.title: Navigating the ethical landscape of artificial intelligence in radiography: a cross-sectional study of radiographers' perspectives
evidence.outcome: Radiographers' familiarity with AI integration in radiography
evidence.effect: Most (44.8%) participants were unfamiliar with the integration of AI into radiography.
evidence.quote: Most (44.8%) participants were unfamiliar with the integration of AI into radiography.

evidence.title: Radiographer Education and Learning in Artificial Intelligence (REAL-AI): A survey of radiographers, radiologists, and students' knowledge of and attitude to education on AI
evidence.outcome: Proportion of imaging staff who received formal AI training
evidence.effect: Only 10.3% had received formal AI training; 29.4% currently using AI in their role, 27% unsure.
evidence.quote: Only 10.3 % had received formal AI training.

evidence.title: Human-centred AI for emergency cardiac care: Evaluating RAPIDx AI with PROLIFERATE_AI
evidence.outcome: Comprehension and usability differences by user experience level
evidence.effect: Registrars had the highest comprehension (median 0.466); residents/interns the lowest (median 0.198). Novices had usability challenges and needed targeted training.
evidence.quote: RAPIDx AI enhances diagnostic accuracy and efficiency for experienced users, but usability challenges for novices highlight the need for targeted training and interface refinements.

evidence.title: Global Adoption, Promotion, Impact, and Deployment of AI in Patient Care, Health Care Delivery, Management, and Health Care Systems Leadership: Cross-Sectional Survey
evidence.outcome: Level of AI training received by health care staff during adoption
evidence.effect: Staff training on AI remains low, and AI adoption communication by executive management is poor; no numeric training rate is given in the abstract.
evidence.quote: Although top managers are mainly responsible for adoption processes, staff training remains low.

evidence.title: Global perspectives of ophthalmologists on artificial intelligence adoption in clinical practice
evidence.venue: International journal of retina and vitreous
evidence.outcome: Ophthalmologists' reported barriers to AI adoption, including lack of training
evidence.effect: Lack of training was the most cited barrier (20.5%); 49.6% reported no knowledge of specific AI tools; 75.1% interested in AI education; only 7.2% reported regular use.
evidence.quote: Key barriers included lack of training (20.5%), implementation costs (16.5%), and reliability concerns (12.9%).

evidence.title: Artificial Intelligence Adoption in Surgery: Cognition, Usage Patterns and Implementation Barriers of DeepSeek Among Healthcare Professionals in China's Tertiary Hospitals
evidence.outcome: Proportion of surgical staff using DeepSeek who had received AI training
evidence.effect: 94.8% of surgical medical staff were untrained on DeepSeek; data privacy concerns 57.5% and over-reliance fears 58.5% were also reported barriers.
evidence.quote: Key barriers include insufficient training (94.8% untrained), data privacy concerns (57.5%) and over-reliance fears (58.5%).

evidence.title: Perceptions of dental students on the integration of artificial intelligence in radiology clinical education
evidence.outcome: Student-reported curriculum preparedness and confidence to use AI caries detection clinically
evidence.effect: Only 16.7% agreed the curriculum adequately prepared them to use AI clinically; 45.5% felt confident integrating AI into future practice. Students requested structured faculty training.
evidence.quote: However, only 16.7% agreed the curriculum adequately prepared them to use AI clinically, and just 45.5% felt confident about integrating AI into future practice.

evidence.title: Evaluation of sepsis CDS tool knowledge and utilization among graduate medical trainees: insights to inform redesign in an academic health system
evidence.outcome: Trainee awareness and use of sepsis CDS tool features
evidence.effect: Among 80 who recognized the sepsis alert, only 11.3% had used the advisor; lack of awareness about advisor features and alert suppression limited engagement.
evidence.quote: Lack of awareness about advisor features and alert suppression mechanisms further limited engagement.

evidence.title: The Utility of Artificial Intelligence in Dermatology Training and Practice: A National, Cross-Sectional Study
evidence.outcome: Proportion of dermatology trainees reporting no formal AI training
evidence.effect: 69.1% reported no formal training; limited training or knowledge cited as a barrier by 52.9%.
evidence.quote: However, 69.1% reported no formal training.

evidence.title: Radiographers' role in the age of AI: A qualitative comparative multi case study
evidence.outcome: Radiographers' formal AI training availability
evidence.effect: Participants reported a lack of training; formal AI training is absent in Sweden and remains limited despite AI in workflows such as image reconstruction, protocol optimisation and patient positioning.
evidence.quote: Participants reported a lack of training and uncertainty about the future, as radiographers' roles are rarely considered in technology implementation.
evidence.sample_unit: interview participants (section leaders, researchers, department managers)

evidence.title: Knowledge, Attitudes, and Training Needs for AI in Primary Care: National Survey Study of Clinicians in the Veterans Health Administration
evidence.outcome: Proportion of PCPs who received any AI training versus those prioritizing AI training
evidence.effect: 88.2% (150/170) identified AI training as a priority, but only 26.5% (45/170) had any training; training experiences varied widely in source, focus, and structure.
evidence.quote: Though 88.2% (150/170) identified AI training as a priority, only 26.5% (45/170) had any training.

evidence.title: Awareness, attitudes, and perceived barriers to artificial intelligence adoption in Turkish clinical biochemistry laboratories: An exploratory cross-sectional survey
evidence.outcome: Proportion of laboratory staff who had received AI-related training
evidence.effect: 57.6% had never received AI-related training; 83.5% cited absence of trained personnel as a barrier; greatest knowledge deficits in image processing (49.4% no knowledge) and predictive analytics (35.9%).
evidence.quote: More than half (57.6%) had never received AI-related training, and current use of AI tools in routine practice was minimal.

evidence.title: Global physician perspectives on artificial intelligence in healthcare across 50 countries and territories
evidence.outcome: Proportion of physicians with formal AI training; association of training with AI use
evidence.effect: 17.7% had received formal training; 27.8% had used AI in practice. Trained physicians were >3 times as likely to use AI (adjusted OR 3.40; 95% CI 2.31-5.01).
evidence.quote: However, only 27.8% had used AI in practice, and 17.7% had received formal training.

evidence.title: Conversational artificial intelligence in the operating room: an exploratory cross-sectional single-center survey among anesthesiology residents
evidence.outcome: Formal training, supervision, and policies for conversational AI use among residents
evidence.effect: Formal training, supervision, and institutional policies appeared limited, while 58.1% of residents used conversational AI in the operating room.
evidence.quote: Formal training, supervision, and institutional policies appeared limited.

evidence.title: Assessing pediatric gastroenterologists' use of artificial intelligence in clinical and professional tasks
evidence.outcome: Proportion of pediatric gastroenterologists who received AI training and desire for more education
evidence.effect: 28.7% received AI training; 84.4% would like more education in the use of AI in practice.
evidence.quote: Few (28.7%) received training in AI, while the majority (84.4%) would like more education in the use of AI in practice.

evidence.title: General-Purpose Artificial Intelligence Use in Routine Mental Health Practice Among Australian Clinicians: Mixed Methods Study
evidence.outcome: Clinician-reported insufficient training or support for AI tools
evidence.effect: Insufficient training or support and limited confidence in judging outputs were among commonly endorsed concerns; no specific percentages given in the abstract.
evidence.quote: Commonly endorsed concerns included privacy and security, accuracy, insufficient training or support, limited confidence in judging outputs, and a preference for human judgment.
evidence.sample_unit: survey respondents (mental health professionals); plus 12 interviewed clinicians

evidence.title: Adoption, perceived value, and barriers to generative artificial intelligence in emergency medicine: A cross-sectional survey of Latin American clinicians
evidence.venue: International journal of critical illness and injury science
evidence.outcome: Availability of structured AI training and interest in formal training
evidence.effect: 88.4% expressed interest in formal AI training; adoption occurred almost entirely without structured training.
evidence.quote: Despite this, 88.4% expressed interest in formal AI training and 65.6% supported integration into clinical guidelines.

evidence.title: Oncologists' knowledge, attitudes and needs about artificial intelligence in clinical oncology in Luxembourg in 2026: a national cross-sectional survey (AICO study)
evidence.outcome: Proportion of oncologists with formal AI training
evidence.effect: 88% (95% CI 70.0-95.8) of 25 respondents had no formal AI training, while all had used LLMs and 20% used them for clinical decision support.
evidence.quote: In total 25 physicians responded (59.5%), 88% (95% CI 70.0-95.8) of whom had no formal AI training.

evidence.title: Physician readiness for artificial intelligence integration in clinical screening and diagnosis: Multicenter cross-sectional study in Jeddah, Saudi Arabia
evidence.outcome: Physician-reported barrier of insufficient AI training and knowledge of AI concepts
evidence.effect: Insufficient training was the most frequently reported barrier (58.9%); only 50.3% demonstrated good knowledge of AI concepts and applications.
evidence.quote: The most frequently reported barriers were insufficient training (58.9%) and lack of trust in AI systems (53.8%).

evidence.title: Artificial Intelligence-Based Chatbots in Genetic Counseling Practice: Current Uptake, Utilization, and Perspectives
evidence.outcome: Proportion of genetic counselors who received AI training
evidence.effect: 16/195 (8.2%) received AI training; limited training identified as a barrier to adoption of chatbots in genetic counseling.
evidence.quote: Limited AI training was identified as a barrier to adoption (16/195; 8.2% received training), highlighting a need for structured education on AI applications in genetic counseling.
evidence.sample_unit: genetic counselors and genetic counseling students surveyed

evidence.title: Exploring the barriers to and facilitators of implementing CanRisk in primary care: a qualitative thematic framework analysis
evidence.venue: The British journal of general practice : the journal of the Royal College of General Practitioners
evidence.outcome: Practitioner confidence and knowledge to use the risk tool
evidence.effect: Lack of confidence and knowledge was a main barrier; PCPs may benefit from CanRisk-specific training.
evidence.quote: PCPs may also benefit from information about cancer risk assessment and CanRisk-specific training.

evidence.title: AI in obstetrics: Evaluating residents' capabilities and interaction strategies with ChatGPT
evidence.venue: European journal of obstetrics, gynecology, and reproductive biology
evidence.outcome: Accuracy of residents' ChatGPT responses on a clinical topic and self-rated AI proficiency
evidence.effect: Low AI proficiency among residents; only 21% accurate responses with third-party questioning due to misinterpreted medical acronyms; most residents dissatisfied with their AI training.
evidence.quote: Interaction with ChatGPT regarding clinical signs of acute hepatic steatosis gravidarum revealed a preference for third-party questioning, resulting in only 21% accurate responses due to misinterpretation of medical acronyms.

evidence.title: Primary Care Provider Preferences Regarding Artificial Intelligence in Point-of-Care Cancer Screening
evidence.outcome: Clinician-reported adequacy of AI training in medical education
evidence.effect: Ninety (>90%) somewhat or strongly agreed that their medical education did not provide adequate AI training.
evidence.quote: Ninety (>90%) somewhat or strongly agreed that their medical education did not provide adequate AI training.

evidence.title: Translating the machine; An assessment of clinician understanding of ophthalmological artificial intelligence outputs
evidence.outcome: Clinicians' self-reported knowledge of interacting with AI and desire for training
evidence.effect: All clinicians had a general consensus on lack of current knowledge in interacting with AI and desired more training.
evidence.quote: All clinicians had a general consensus on lack of current knowledge in interacting with AI and desire more training.

evidence.title: Quantifying the AI readiness gap: An international, multidisciplinary assessment of artificial intelligence literacy in the radiation oncology community
evidence.outcome: AI literacy knowledge among radiation oncology staff, including model mechanics and prediction uncertainty
evidence.effect: Widespread deficits in fundamental model mechanics and interpretation of prediction uncertainty; Medical Physicists scored higher than Radiation Oncologists and Radiation Therapists (p < 0.001).
evidence.quote: However, required competencies vary by role. While the workforce exhibited strong intuition regarding data-centric risks such as bias and data drift, widespread deficits were identified in fundamental model mechanics and interpretation of prediction uncertainty.
evidence.sample_unit: respondents completing all items of the AI literacy assessment

evidence.title: Perception and challenges of artificial intelligence (AI) in Emergency Medicine: A multi-country study in Sub-Saharan Africa
evidence.venue: African journal of emergency medicine : Revue africaine de la medecine d'urgence
evidence.outcome: Proportion of emergency clinicians who had received formal AI training
evidence.effect: Only 14.2% had received formal training; 88.2% had basic AI understanding; 64.5% named training as the most critical support need.
evidence.quote: Most respondents had a basic understanding of AI (88.2 %) and were aware of AI applications in emergency medicine (73.2 %), yet only 14.2 % had received formal training.
evidence.sample_unit: emergency medicine consultants and residents (survey responses)

evidence.title: Artificial Intelligence Integration in Radiology in Saudi Arabia: A Cross-Sectional Survey of Workforce Readiness and Implementation Challenges
evidence.outcome: Perceived barriers to AI integration in radiology, including insufficient staff training
evidence.effect: Insufficient staff training rated a major barrier (3.84 ± 0.77) and lack of technical expertise (3.82 ± 0.78); implementation readiness was lower (3.04 ± 0.79).
evidence.quote: Major barriers included implementation costs (3.98 ± 0.71), limited digital infrastructure (3.90 ± 0.75), insufficient staff training (3.84 ± 0.77), and lack of technical expertise (3.82 ± 0.78).
evidence.sample_unit: healthcare professionals involved in radiology services

commentary.bottom_line: Fifteen studies suggest that tool-specific training is associated with gains in knowledge, tool use, and some care processes, but most lack a comparison group and the one real-deployment trial bundled training with ongoing implementation support. Certainty that training by itself prevents misoperation or patient harm is low.

perspectives.view: One real-deployment cluster RCT (n=9155) reports repeat BP measurement aOR 3.45 with in-person plus online training and monthly check-ins versus online-only training, but training was not isolated from implementation support. Most other studies use uncontrolled pre-post designs with knowledge outcomes. Risk of bias, indirectness, and bundled interventions support a low certainty rating.

Few studies measure errors that reach patients. In Sierra Leone, 84.6% of first-time users of a tutorial-equipped app produced sufficient scans versus 31.0% without tutorials (OR 12.2), a result confounded with facility type. After one-hour training in Australia, knowledge scores ranged from 36.8% to 84.2%, which suggests confidence may exceed understanding of limitations.

Short formats appear workable. A 2-hour session preceded a 23.3% time saving per case, and a 10-minute LLM tutorial raised resident top-three accuracy to 62.5% from 44.8% in simulation. Only 14% of hematologists using clinical AI reported structured training, and dietitian interviews point to staff turnover as a reason training must continue after go-live.

Rural settings appear in the American cluster RCT and the Sierra Leone scan study, and a course in Guyana and Nigeria raised knowledge scores from 75% to 95% among 30 radiology residents and attendings. No test enrolled Medicaid, safety-net, or low-literacy populations, and no study tested the education of disadvantaged patient subgroups that the HEAAL framework describes.

One endorsing source states that the cost of adopting a technology exceeds its purchase cost, citing staffing and change management. A single 2-hour session sufficed for one French team, but the trial effect came with monthly check-ins and feedback, and 52.6% of Australian staff wanted more post-training support. Budgets may need to cover support beyond go-live.

Patient-level results are sparse. Hypertension recognition improved (aOR 2.31) in the rural trial, and Xpert-confirmed TB per 100,000 radiographs rose from 858 to 2112 in Vietnam without a comparison group. The only patient satisfaction data come from practitioners' self-reported perceptions, so no study reports what patients themselves experienced.

commentary.research_gap: No controlled study isolates use-case-specific training from other implementation support while measuring misoperation, misapplied outputs, or patient harm. Trials are needed that compare training formats and refresher schedules, track retention as staff turn over, and enroll Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, and low-literacy settings in the United States.
commentary.underserved_note: Two tests included rural populations (the American cluster RCT and the Sierra Leone scan study), one included low-income settings (Guyana and Nigeria), and the Sierra Leone study was also tagged as a non-English setting, though that label describes the provider context rather than patients with limited English proficiency in American health care. No test included Medicaid, safety-net, or low-literacy populations, so the findings may not transfer to the settings where misapplied outputs could compound existing disparities.
